title: AI startup hacked Anthropic, gains access to employee details, internal messages
content:
AI startup claims it hacked Anthropic in 12 hours, gains access to employee details and internal messages
Agents found a way in through third-party business software
- AI startup Cathedral used autonomous agents to breach Anthropic systems through weaknesses in third-party software
- Agents accessed HR, sales, and IT data, exposing limited customer and partner information
- Incident highlights how AI-powered attackers can rapidly exploit vendor weaknesses despite strong internal defenses
An AI startup seemingly gave Anthropic a taste of its own medicine when it used AI agents to break into the company and expose sensitive data.
The company in question is called Cathedral, which was founded by former members of the defunct US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a US government initiative established to reduce federal spending and bureaucracy, while modernizing government technology and operations.
Anthropic is running a two-fold bug bounty program through HackerOne. One part is focused on finding technical flaws in Anthropic’s systems, while the other is an invite-only program that rewards researchers for finding universal jailbreaks that bypass Claude’s safety protections.
Cathedral apparently shared its results with Anthropic through the bug bounty program. After its human researchers unsuccessfully tried breaking in for a few days, they deployed AI agents which took less than 12 hours to find a way in, by exploiting flaws in third-party business software.
Violating the rules
After accessing the company’s network, the agents accessed meeting transcripts, information on salaries and job offers, as well as Slack messages. Employee conversations with Claude were not exposed, it seems.
Anthropic confirmed the news, saying Cathedral accessed a “limited set” of sales, human resources, and IT systems, and compromised contact information and basic user account records belonging to certain customers and partners. Source code and AI model weights were not accessed.
“Our monitoring flagged some of Cathedral’s activity before they reported it to us,” Anthropic said in a statement shared with The Washington Post. “We shut off their access the same day.”

According to Gizmodo, Anthropic accused Cathedral of violating the program’s rules by failing to disclose the full extent of its activity. We don’t know if that means Anthropic won’t release the payment for the bounty, but it sure sounds like it.
Paying the bounty could be the least of Anthropic’s concerns, though. The company is currently gearing up for its Initial Public Offering (IPO), with a valuation of $1.4 billion. Leaking sensitive data to anyone, including white hat hackers, is definitely not a good signal.
A 'bunch of kids' wreaking havoc
“The fact that weaknesses in ordinary enterprise software can compromise the infrastructure of even the most advanced organizations should be a wake-up call for every company in America,” the Washington Post cited Cathedral’s report as saying.
At the same time, a senior Trump administration official allegedly told Via The Independentthat “if a bunch of kids who have just started a company can do this, then potentially the Chinese aren’t far behind.”
Cathedral can hardly be described as “a bunch of kids” - it is an AI startup focused on offensive and defensive cyber operations for the US military and government. Its founders include Gavin Kliger (former Pentagon chief data officer), Luke Farritor (best known for helping decipher ancient Roman scrolls using machine learning), Marko Elez (former SpaceX staffer), and Jack Stein (apparently worked as an investment banking associate at Salem Partners before joining DOGE).
The cybersecurity community had something to say about it. Jacob Krell, Senior Director for Secure AI Solutions & Cybersecurity at Suzu Labs, wasn’t particularly phased, saying if third-party vendors are a risk everywhere, then they’re a risk at Anthropic.
"Cathedral's agents got into Anthropic the same way attackers get into everyone else, through the vendors,” Krell said. “Security maturity is capped by the weakest vendor you integrate with, and no amount of in-house engineering changes that."
Darin Fredde, Senior Director of Technical Marketing Engineering at Ridge Security, praised Anthropic’s response: "Anthropic deserves credit for reporting that its monitoring detected some of the activity and for taking containment measures. But the real measure of remediation is independent verification that those attack paths are closed. We need to stop confusing a successful patch with a verified security outcome. Otherwise, we're just closing the front door and hoping nobody discovered the spare key."

report.summary: AI startup Cathedral used autonomous agents to breach Anthropic via third-party software, accessing employee and limited partner data before being shut down.
report.background: Anthropic runs a two-track bug bounty on HackerOne: one for technical flaws, one invite-only for universal Claude jailbreaks. Cathedral, founded by former DOGE members and focused on offensive and defensive cyber operations for the US military and government, participated after its human researchers failed for days. Its AI agents found a route in under 12 hours by exploiting weaknesses in third-party business software. The incident comes as AI companies face rising scrutiny over supply-chain security and as Anthropic prepares for an IPO. The breach did not touch source code or model weights, but exposed HR, sales and IT data plus limited customer and partner records. Anthropic says monitoring flagged some activity before Cathedral reported it and access was cut the same day. Anthropic also accused Cathedral of violating bounty rules by not fully disclosing its activity, raising questions about how AI-powered offensive security work is governed.
key_points: Cathedral’s autonomous agents breached Anthropic in under 12 hours after human researchers failed for days, entering through flaws in third-party business software rather than Anthropic’s core defenses. The agents then reached meeting transcripts, salary and job-offer data, Slack messages, and limited customer and partner contact records.

Anthropic confirmed access to a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems but said source code and AI model weights were not exposed. Its monitoring flagged some activity before Cathedral reported the issue, and Anthropic shut off access the same day.

The exercise was submitted through Anthropic’s HackerOne bug bounty, but Anthropic accused Cathedral of violating program rules by failing to disclose the full extent of its activity. That dispute could affect bounty payment and highlights governance gaps in AI-powered offensive research.

Security experts say the breach underscores vendor risk: an organization’s security maturity is capped by the weakest third-party software it integrates. AI agents can accelerate discovery and exploitation of ordinary enterprise software weaknesses, making supply-chain security a board-level concern.

Cathedral is not a random group of hobbyists: its founders include former DOGE, Pentagon, SpaceX and finance staff, and it targets offensive and defensive cyber for US military and government. A Trump administration official reportedly warned that if a new startup can do this, foreign adversaries may not be far behind.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the incident shows that model safety and strong internal engineering are not enough when third-party SaaS remains an attack surface. Autonomous agents lower the cost and time needed to find and exploit vendor weaknesses, pressuring AI companies to verify patches independently and clearly scope bug bounty activity. For developers, it reinforces least privilege, vendor risk reviews, network segmentation and monitoring for anomalous agent behavior, especially around HR, sales and IT data. For regular users, exposed contact and account records can fuel targeted phishing, while employee Slack and salary data create privacy and trust risks. The breach may accelerate demand for AI-driven security testing, supply-chain assurance and clearer rules for offensive AI agents before they become routine.
report.tools: Follow Anthropic’s HackerOne bug bounty for disclosure details, and watch HackerOne and Bugcrowd for bounty program governance. For defensive testing, consider OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, Nuclei and Semgrep for web and application scanning, plus vendor risk management and attack surface management platforms. Open-source SIEM like Wazuh and emerging AI-agent security frameworks can help monitor anomalous agent activity. Treat these as defensive tools, not intrusion aids.
